name: Surveyor 3
shortDescription: NASA's Surveyor 3 was the second Surveyor spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on the Moon. Its surface-sampling experiments demonstrated that lunar soil was strong enough to support an Apollo Lunar Module.
overview: Surveyor 3 was the third engineering flight in NASA's Surveyor program and the first to carry a surface-sampling instrument capable of digging into lunar soil. Landing in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum on April 20, 1967, the spacecraft transmitted 6,326 television images and conducted experiments to measure the strength and consistency of the lunar surface. Its findings confirmed that the Moon's surface could support the weight of an Apollo Lunar Module. In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Charles Conrad Jr. and Alan L. Bean visited the inactive lander and recovered parts of its camera system and soil sampler for examination on Earth.
historicalStory: During the 1960s, NASA needed to establish whether the lunar surface could safely support astronauts and the Apollo Lunar Module. Surveyor 3 was designed to investigate this question through direct experiments on the Moon. Launched on April 17, 1967, aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket, it began its journey following a burn from the Centaur upper stage after reaching Earth parking orbit. During lunar descent, highly reflective rocks confused the spacecraft's descent radar, preventing its main engine from shutting down at the correct altitude. The lander bounced twice, reaching heights of approximately 33 feet (10 meters) and 10 feet (3 meters), before finally settling on the lunar surface at 00:04:17 UT on April 20, 1967. It landed in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum, approximately 3 degrees south latitude and 23.41 degrees west longitude. Less than an hour after landing, Surveyor 3 began transmitting television images of its surroundings. Its surface sampler reached up to 5 feet (1.5 meters) from the spacecraft and dug trenches as deep as 7 inches (18 centimeters). Through four trenching operations, four bearing tests, and thirteen impact tests, scientists determined that lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand and a bearing strength of approximately 10 pounds per square inch (98 kilopascals). These findings demonstrated that the lunar surface could support an Apollo Lunar Module. Surveyor 3 transmitted its final communication on May 4, 1967, two days after lunar night began. More than two years later, on November 19, 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Charles Conrad Jr. and Alan L. Bean visited the lander during their second extravehicular activity. They recovered components, including the soil scoop and television camera system, allowing scientists to examine the effects of prolonged exposure to the lunar environment.
purpose: To achieve a soft landing on the Moon, investigate the physical properties and bearing strength of lunar soil, conduct surface-sampling experiments, and capture television images of the lunar environment in preparation for future Apollo landings.

missionTimeline.title: Launch from Cape Canaveral
missionTimeline.description: Launched aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket from Launch Complex 36B at Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 07:05:01 UT.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Soft Landing
missionTimeline.description: After bouncing twice because of a descent radar malfunction, the spacecraft successfully landed in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum at 00:04:17 UT.

missionTimeline.title: First Television Transmissions
missionTimeline.description: Began transmitting images of the surrounding lunar landscape less than an hour after landing.

missionTimeline.title: Surface Sampling Experiments
missionTimeline.description: Conducted four trenching operations, four bearing tests, and thirteen impact tests to investigate lunar soil properties.

missionTimeline.title: Final Communication
missionTimeline.description: Transmitted its last signal two days after the beginning of lunar night.

missionTimeline.title: Apollo 12 Landing Nearby
missionTimeline.description: Apollo 12 astronauts Charles Conrad Jr. and Alan L. Bean landed approximately 180 meters from Surveyor 3 aboard the Intrepid Lunar Module.

missionTimeline.title: Astronaut Inspection and Sample Recovery
missionTimeline.description: During their second lunar EVA, Conrad and Bean visited Surveyor 3 and recovered its soil scoop and television camera components for examination on Earth.

achievements: Successfully demonstrated that lunar soil could support the weight of an Apollo Lunar Module.
Transmitted 6,326 television images of the lunar surface.
Performed four soil-trenching operations, four bearing tests, and thirteen impact tests.
Became the first Surveyor spacecraft to carry and operate a surface-sampling instrument.
Was visited by Apollo 12 astronauts, who recovered spacecraft components for scientific examination on Earth.

location.description: Landed in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum at approximately 3 degrees south latitude and 23.41 degrees west longitude.

developmentNote: Coordinates are based on the approximate landing location reported in NASA's mission account. The supplied NASA source does not establish the previous dummy data's more precise coordinate claim.
equipmentStatus: Inactive / Historic spacecraft remaining on the lunar surface
whyLeftBehind: Surveyor 3 was an uncrewed lunar lander designed to conduct surface experiments. It had no capability to launch itself back to Earth. The spacecraft remained on the Moon after completing its mission and was later visited by Apollo 12 astronauts, who recovered selected components for analysis.
interestingFacts: Surveyor 3 bounced twice during its descent, reaching approximately 33 feet (10 meters) and 10 feet (3 meters) before finally landing.
Its surface sampler could reach up to 5 feet (1.5 meters) from the lander and dig approximately 7 inches (18 centimeters) into lunar soil.
The spacecraft performed four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests to investigate the mechanical properties of lunar soil.
Apollo 12 astronauts landed approximately 180 meters from Surveyor 3 and visited it during their second lunar EVA.
The recovered camera and soil sampler components allowed scientists to investigate the effects of extended lunar exposure on spacecraft materials.

name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module (Eagle)
shortDescription: The descent stage of Apollo 11's Lunar Module Eagle carried the first humans to the lunar surface. After Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin returned to lunar orbit, the descent stage was left behind and its eventual fate remains unknown.
overview: Apollo 11's Lunar Module, named Eagle, was the first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon. It carried Commander Neil A. Armstrong and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. to the lunar surface on July 20, 1969. The Lunar Module consisted of two stages: the descent stage, which provided the landing platform, and the ascent stage, which returned the astronauts to the Command and Service Module. After the astronauts completed their lunar surface activities, the ascent stage lifted off and the descent stage was left behind.
historicalStory: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 made history when the Lunar Module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility. Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UT on July 21, followed by Buzz Aldrin 19 minutes later. During their approximately two-and-a-half-hour surface activity, they collected lunar samples, photographed the landscape, deployed scientific equipment, raised an American flag, and unveiled a commemorative plaque. After completing their work, the astronauts returned to Eagle and prepared for departure. The ascent stage lifted off on July 21, leaving the descent stage behind. The eventual fate of the descent stage is unknown, although NASA's archive assumes it crashed onto the Moon within the following one to four months.
purpose: The Lunar Module was designed to transport astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and return them to the Command and Service Module. Its descent stage provided the landing propulsion, landing legs, and equipment storage. It also served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the astronauts back into lunar orbit.

missionTimeline.title: Launch from Earth
missionTimeline.description: Apollo 11 launched from Cape Canaveral aboard a Saturn V rocket.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Module Separation
missionTimeline.description: The Lunar Module undocked from the Command and Service Module before beginning its descent toward the lunar surface.

missionTimeline.title: The Eagle Has Landed
missionTimeline.description: The Lunar Module landed in Mare Tranquillitatis, the Sea of Tranquility, at 20:17:40 UT.

missionTimeline.title: First Human Moonwalk
missionTimeline.description: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UT, followed by Buzz Aldrin 19 minutes later.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Surface Exploration
missionTimeline.description: The astronauts collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil, photographed the surroundings, deployed scientific experiments, and traversed approximately 250 meters.

missionTimeline.title: Return to Lunar Orbit
missionTimeline.description: The Lunar Module ascent stage lifted off at 17:54:01 UT after 21 hours and 36 minutes on the lunar surface.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Module Jettison
missionTimeline.description: After docking with the Command and Service Module, the Lunar Module was jettisoned into lunar orbit. Its eventual fate is unknown.

achievements: First crewed vehicle to land on the Moon.
Carried the first two humans to walk on the lunar surface.
Enabled the first human lunar exploration and geological sample collection.
Supported the collection of 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil.
Provided the landing platform and launch system that enabled the astronauts to return to lunar orbit.
Marked the beginning of human exploration of the lunar surface.

location.coordinateAccuracy: NASA coordinates determined from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images using the DE 421 reference frame
location.description: The Apollo 11 landing site is located in Mare Tranquillitatis, also known as the Sea of Tranquility, on the Moon.

developmentNote: This entry represents only the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, not the ascent stage or the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP). NASA's archive does not establish the exact final resting place of the descent stage. Map layout coordinates have not been provided and must be assigned during UI development.
equipmentStatus: Descent stage jettisoned into lunar orbit on July 22, 1969. Its eventual fate is unknown; NASA's archive assumes it crashed onto the lunar surface within one to four months.
whyLeftBehind: The Lunar Module consisted of two stages. The descent stage provided the landing platform and supported lunar surface operations. After the astronauts completed their activities, the ascent stage lifted off to return them to the Command and Service Module. The descent stage was no longer needed and remained behind. Its later fate is uncertain.
interestingFacts: The Lunar Module was named Eagle.
It carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, the first two humans to walk on the Moon.
Armstrong announced the successful landing with the famous words, 'Houston, Tranquility Base here - the Eagle has landed.'
The complete Lunar Module had a mass of 15,103 kg, including propellants.
The descent stage was approximately 4.2 meters across and 1.7 meters thick.
The descent stage had four landing legs with round footpads.
The astronauts spent 21 hours and 36 minutes on the lunar surface.
The astronauts traveled approximately 250 meters during their lunar surface exploration.
The descent stage's exact final resting place is unknown.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module (Falcon)
shortDescription: The descent stage of Apollo 15's Lunar Module Falcon remains on the Moon at the foot of the Apennine Mountains. It served as the landing platform and launch base for the ascent stage that returned the astronauts to lunar orbit.
overview: Apollo 15's Lunar Module, named Falcon, was the fourth crewed vehicle to land on the Moon. It carried Commander David R. Scott and Lunar Module Pilot James B. Irwin to the lunar surface on July 30, 1971. The spacecraft consisted of two stages. After the astronauts completed their lunar surface activities, the ascent stage lifted off to rendezvous with the Command and Service Module. The descent stage remained behind at the landing site in the Mare Imbrium region.
historicalStory: Apollo 15 marked an important step in human lunar exploration. During three moonwalks totaling 18 hours and 35 minutes, David Scott and James Irwin explored the lunar landscape, collected geological samples, and conducted scientific investigations. The mission introduced the Lunar Roving Vehicle on a crewed lunar mission, allowing the astronauts to explore areas farther from their landing site. After their surface activities, the astronauts departed in the Lunar Module's ascent stage. The descent stage remained on the Moon as a physical reminder of the mission and its achievements.
purpose: The Lunar Module was designed to transport astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and return them to the Command and Service Module. Its descent stage provided the landing system, propulsion, storage space, and a platform for the ascent stage. After the astronauts completed their surface operations, the descent stage was left on the lunar surface.

missionTimeline.title: Launch from Earth
missionTimeline.description: Apollo 15 launched from Cape Canaveral aboard a Saturn V rocket.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Landing
missionTimeline.description: The Lunar Module Falcon landed in the Mare Imbrium region at the foot of the Apennine Mountains.

missionTimeline.title: First Stand-up EVA
missionTimeline.description: Approximately two hours after landing, David Scott performed a 33-minute stand-up EVA to describe and photograph the surrounding terrain.

missionTimeline.title: First Moonwalk
missionTimeline.description: Scott and Irwin deployed and drove the Lunar Roving Vehicle, collected geological samples, and explored the area around Hadley Rille.

missionTimeline.title: Second Moonwalk
missionTimeline.description: The astronauts drove the Lunar Roving Vehicle southeast along the Apennine Mountains, exploring several craters and collecting samples.

missionTimeline.title: Final Moonwalk
missionTimeline.description: The astronauts completed their third EVA, exploring Scarp Crater and the edge of Hadley Rille. Scott also performed the televised hammer-and-feather demonstration.

missionTimeline.title: Ascent Stage Departure
missionTimeline.description: The Lunar Module ascent stage lifted off at 17:11:22 UT after 66 hours and 55 minutes on the lunar surface. The descent stage remained behind.

missionTimeline.title: Lunar Module Jettison
missionTimeline.description: After docking with the Command and Service Module, the ascent stage was jettisoned and later impacted the Moon.

achievements: Fourth crewed vehicle to land on the Moon.
First Apollo mission to use a Lunar Roving Vehicle.
Enabled astronauts to explore regions within approximately 5 km of the landing site.
Supported three moonwalks totaling 18 hours and 35 minutes.
Enabled the collection of 77.31 kg of lunar rock and soil samples.
Provided a landing and launch platform for the astronauts' lunar surface operations.

location.coordinateAccuracy: NASA coordinates determined from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images using the DE 421 reference frame
location.description: The landing site is in the Mare Imbrium region at the foot of the Apennine mountain range on the Moon.

developmentNote: The record covers the Apollo 15 Lunar Module and its associated ALSEP experiments. This entry intentionally focuses only on the Lunar Module descent stage. Map layout coordinates have not been provided and must be assigned during UI development.
equipmentStatus: Descent stage remains on the lunar surface. Its original operational purpose ended when the ascent stage departed on August 2, 1971.
whyLeftBehind: The Lunar Module consisted of a descent stage and an ascent stage. The descent stage provided the landing platform and supported the ascent stage during lunar surface operations. Once the astronauts completed their activities, the ascent stage launched to return them to lunar orbit, leaving the descent stage behind on the Moon.
interestingFacts: The Lunar Module was named Falcon.
It carried astronauts David R. Scott and James B. Irwin.
The complete Lunar Module had an initial mass of 16,430 kg, including propellants.
The descent stage was approximately 4.2 meters across and 1.7 meters thick.
The descent stage had four landing legs with round footpads.
The astronauts spent 66 hours and 55 minutes on the lunar surface.
The Lunar Roving Vehicle was used for the first time on a crewed lunar mission.
